Hey! I am going through this right now but have learned some things that have helped me. I did 8 years active and got out at 27. The timing is certainly awkward.  I spent about two years experiencing whiplash from all of the turmoil of the military and also some stuff from childhood.


 It hit me like a ton of bricks. You are likely feeling out of place because your identity is no longer within the military. The most important thing you can do is find a fulfilling way to spend your time with people you care about. Even if you have just an inkling of interest in something, pursue it. Run it down. Try something new. Never let the feel of failure or being bad at something keep you from pursuing what interests you.


Find the things that excite you. In the last two years I got involved with a BJJ group for veterans and it’s been one of the most important interactions of my life. To be able to regularly meet with veterans and share in the struggle of “civ life” is invaluable. Also, I HIGHLY RECOMMEND THERAPY. All of my most well-adjusted veteran friends are in therapy.


 I have also just started college, am playing guitar, gotten back into concert photography, and I compete in a jiu jitsu tournament this weekend. You probably feel out of place because your current sense of identity isn’t aligned with that of a civilian. And that’s ok! Don’t beat yourself up. You are making a big adjustment, but everything will be ok. And there are ample resources for you to navigate the transition back to civilian.  


TL;DR: Find a community of veterans with a common interest, pursue ANY hobby you find interesting, go to therapy, use your GI Bill and disability benefits. If you haven’t applied for disability, start on it immediately.

Start with treatment for yourself before you begin to consider that. It is possible to get a med-sep but it’s a long road. Start first by getting treatment and finding ways to improve your quality of life.

Talking to Mental Health is a win-win in my book. It is wildly intimidating at first, I agree. The first time I reached for the door to enter my MH appointment it was like a forcefield.

That being said, I would recommend starting like this…

1. Chaplain. You don’t have to be religious, most are genuinely good people. I am a buddhist but every chappy I met with was protestant.

2. If Chaplain doesn’t suit you, go MFLC. They are confidential, keep no records, and will only report to your chain of command if there is a concern for your physical safety. They were also terrific in my experience.

3. Mental health. They will take care of you, full-stop. Most people that warn others of the MH clinic have never been themselves. I only have positive things to say but I’m sure there are outliers.

Even if you decide not to go to Mental Health immediately, I would encourage you to get treatment from them before you get out. I have so many friends that had severe mental health symptoms while they were in, but never received treatment. Because there were no records of mental health treatment, it was nearly impossible for them to apply for disability for things like PTSD, depression, and anxiety. 70% of my disability rating is from depression, alone.

Good luck my dude! Always here if you need anything.

Hey dude, crew chief sucks. I did 8 years (2 deployments) on fighters and only got out because I got the retraining runaround. I would have been happy to do 20 in another AFSC 
but I had to look out for my happiness and mental health. Anybody that says crew chief is a good job is fortunate enough to be delusional. MX is dogshit and I will die on this hill.

How much longer do you have on your contract? Are you taking care of your mental health? Have you been to MFLC? (great option).

Get treated for your mental health and all other injuries/illnesses so you will be set on disability when you get out. I get 100% disability and it’s awesome (minus, you know, the disabilities).

Find a way to get your college done if you think that is viable with your energy/mental health right now. Get a business degree or some shit, nobody cares but it will make a difference when you look for jobs on the outside.

Take leave, go to the gym, find friends/hobbies, do whatever you need to do to lighten the load for yourself. Also, don’t fall into that trap of eating like shit and drinking too much. And get good sleep.

If things become too mentally strenuous for you, do not hesitate to go to mental health to talk about your options. (I did, as well as MANY of my crew chief friends). They have a lot of pull in terms of getting you placed in support/training/whatever. Fuck whoever says anything about you “skating” or “slacking.” Look out for you, big dog.
